MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures & Swabs:
Blood cultures detect bacteraemia or fungaemia by growing organisms directly from the bloodstream. They are a core part of the Sepsis 6 and should be taken BEFORE antibiotics — but in septic shock you must never delay antibiotics beyond the recommended window to chase a sample. Correct technique is what makes the result interpretable: contamination and inadequate volume are the two commonest reasons a culture misleads.
1Technique determines validity
A blood culture is only as good as how it was drawn. Get these right and the result can be trusted.
  • Strict asepsis (ANTT) with thorough skin antisepsis (chlorhexidine in alcohol) — the single best defence against contaminants.
  • Adequate volume is the main determinant of yield — aim for ~8–10 mL per adult bottle; under-filling causes false negatives.
  • Ideally two sets from separate venepuncture sites — this is what lets you judge contaminant vs true pathogen.
  • Fill both the aerobic and anaerobic bottles.
Avoid drawing from an existing indwelling line unless specifically investigating line infection (paired peripheral + line cultures).
2Contaminant vs true pathogen
The key interpretive question. Use the organism, the number of sets positive, and the time-to-positivity (TTP).
🧫Usually contaminant
Coagulase-negative staph (e.g. Staph epidermidis), skin diphtheroids/Corynebacterium, Cutibacterium/Propionibacterium — especially if only 1 of 2 sets positive with long TTP.
🩸Almost never contaminant
Staph aureus, Strep pneumoniae, E. coli/Enterobacterales, Candida — treat as real in any set until proven otherwise.
Same organism in BOTH sets, short TTP→True pathogen
CoNS in 1 of 2 sets, long TTP→Likely contaminant
3What specific isolates mean
Certain positives trigger a defined workup, not just antibiotics.
Staph aureus bacteraemia (SAB)Candidaemia
  • SAB mandates a search for a deep focus / endocarditis (echocardiography), removal of any lines, and repeat cultures to confirm clearance.
  • Relevant/persistent Candida = candidaemia → remove lines, echocardiography, and ophthalmology review for endophthalmitis.
  • In both SAB and candidaemia, repeat cultures to document that the blood has cleared.
🚩
Take cultures before antibiotics but never delay treatment in sepsis/septic shock to obtain them. Staph aureus bacteraemia is never ignored — always hunt for endocarditis or a line/deep-tissue source, remove lines, and repeat cultures. Escalate any septic patient promptly. See Sepsis ›
📷 Image placeholder — paired aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles with a lab report showing organism, number of sets positive, and time-to-positivity annotated.
🎓 Exam pearl. Volume is the biggest driver of yield and two sets from separate sites is what lets you call contaminant vs pathogen. CoNS in 1 of 2 sets with long TTP = likely skin contaminant; Staph aureus in any set = real, so image for endocarditis, pull lines, and repeat cultures to prove clearance.
Urine MC&S (Microscopy, Culture & Sensitivity) is the definitive urine test that identifies the causative organism and its antibiotic sensitivities. Always send a clean-catch midstream specimen (MSU) before antibiotics; it guides targeted therapy in complicated, recurrent, pregnant or treatment-failure UTIs where a dipstick alone is not enough.
1What the three parts tell you
The lab reports microscopy, then culture, then sensitivities.
🔬Microscopy
WBCs (pyuria) = inflammation; RBCs = haematuria; organisms seen; casts suggest renal source; many epithelial cells = contamination.
🧫Culture
Significant bacteriuria is classically ≥10⁵ CFU/mL of a single organism, but lower counts count if there are symptoms or pyuria.
💊Sensitivities
Antibiotic susceptibility (S/I/R) lets you rationalise empirical therapy to a targeted agent.
A high squamous epithelial cell count points to skin/genital contamination — repeat with a proper clean-catch MSU.
2Know your organisms
The commonest cause of UTI is E. coli. Learn the pattern-spotters:
Alkaline urine + struvite (staghorn) stones→Proteus (urease-producing)
Sexually active young woman, coagulase-negative→Staph saprophyticus
Other Gram-negative coliforms→Klebsiella, other coliforms
Dipstick: nitrites (coliforms reduce nitrate)Leucocyte esterase (pyuria)
3Sterile pyuria — a classic finals trap
Sterile pyuria = raised urinary WBCs with a negative routine culture. Don't dismiss it — work through the causes:
  • TB of the renal tract — send early-morning urines for AFB/culture
  • Chlamydia/urethritis and other STIs
  • Prior or partially treated UTI (recent antibiotics)
  • Renal stones or interstitial nephritis
  • Indwelling catheter
4Do NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria
A positive culture in a well, asymptomatic patient usually does not need antibiotics — treating it drives resistance without benefit. This is especially true in the elderly and the catheterised, where colonisation is the norm; don't over-rely on a dipstick or culture to explain non-specific illness. The two exceptions where you do treat:
🤰Pregnancy
Screen and treat — reduces risk of pyelonephritis and preterm labour.
🔧Pre-urological procedure
Treat before TURP/instrumentation that breaches the mucosa.
See related: Urinary tract infection ›
🚩
Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy — untreated it risks pyelonephritis and preterm birth. And in any patient, fever, rigors, loin pain or hypotension with a positive MSU signals urosepsis/pyelonephritis — take blood cultures and start empirical IV antibiotics urgently per the sepsis pathway.
📷 Image placeholder — urine microscopy field showing numerous white blood cells (pyuria) alongside rod-shaped bacilli, contrasted with a contaminated sample showing multiple squamous epithelial cells.
🎓 Exam pearl. Two facts win marks: (1) Don't treat asymptomatic bacteriuria — except in pregnancy or before urological instrumentation/TURP. (2) Sterile pyuria → think TB (early-morning urines for AFB) and chlamydia. Always send a clean-catch MSU before antibiotics, and remember Proteus links to alkaline urine and struvite stones.
A sputum culture & sensitivity identifies bacterial pathogens in the lower respiratory tract and provides antibiotic sensitivities to guide targeted therapy. It is used in pneumonia (especially severe or non-responding), infective exacerbations of COPD and bronchiectasis, and in suspected tuberculosis. Crucially, results are only meaningful when interpreted alongside sample quality and the clinical picture — empirical antibiotics are usually started before cultures return.
1Sample quality is everything
A good specimen is purulent (deep cough, green/yellow) not salivary. The lab grades quality on the Gram film before culturing:
Many epithelial cells + few neutrophils→Saliva / upper-airway contamination — poor sample, reject
Many neutrophils + few epithelial cells→Good lower-respiratory sample — proceed to culture
Normal upper-airway flora (viridans streptococci, Neisseria spp., Candida) is reported as commensal growth — do not treat it.
2Common pathogens by context
🫁CAP / COPD
Strep pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
🦠Bronchiectasis / CF
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staph aureus
🍺Alcoholic / cavitating
Klebsiella pneumoniae (upper-lobe cavitation, 'redcurrant jelly' sputum)
Interpret growth with sample quality and the clinical picture — see Pneumonia ›.
3Atypicals DON'T grow on routine culture
A classic trap: atypical organisms are absent from routine agar — a negative culture does not exclude them. Send a specific atypical screen instead:
Legionella & pneumococcal urinary antigenMycoplasma / Chlamydophila serology or PCR
Mycoplasma, Legionella and Chlamydophila lack a conventional cell wall / need special media — hence the separate tests.
4Suspected TB — a different pathway
Send at least three deep-cough specimens (ideally including an early-morning sample). Each is processed three ways:
  • AFB smear — Ziehl-Neelsen / auramine stain; rapid but low sensitivity.
  • Mycobacterial culture — gold standard, gives full sensitivities, but takes weeks (slow-growing).
  • NAAT / GeneXpert — rapid (hours), also detects rifampicin resistance.
If unable to expectorate, use induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage.
🚩
Suspected TB: place the patient in a negative-pressure side room with airborne (respiratory) isolation before results return, and notify the health protection team — TB is a statutorily notifiable disease. Separately, never delay empirical antibiotics in severe pneumonia (e.g. CURB-65 ≥3) while waiting for culture.
📷 Image placeholder — split figure: (left) a Gram film of a good purulent sample showing sheets of neutrophils with Gram-positive diplococci; (right) a Ziehl-Neelsen smear showing red acid-fast bacilli against a blue background.
🎓 Exam pearl. Two high-yield hooks: (1) Atypicals and TB do not grow on routine sputum culture — a negative routine culture never excludes them; order urinary antigens/serology for atypicals and AFB smear + mycobacterial culture + NAAT for TB. (2) Always check the reported sample quality first — growth from a salivary specimen (many epithelial cells) reflects contamination, and commensal upper-airway flora should never be treated. Start empirical therapy guided by CURB-65, then de-escalate once sensitivities return.
Stool culture and microscopy is the core investigation for infective diarrhoea, used to identify a pathogen when the illness is severe, prolonged, high-risk, or part of an outbreak. Most acute gastroenteritis is viral and self-limiting (norovirus/rotavirus) and needs no culture — testing is targeted, not routine. Crucially, several key tests must be specifically requested: routine culture will not detect C. difficile toxin or parasites unless you ask for them.
1What each request actually detects
A standard stool sample is processed differently depending on what you tick. Order the right test for the clinical picture — a single "stool sample" is not one test but several.
🦠Bacterial culture
Campylobacter (commonest UK bacterial cause), Salmonella, Shigella, and E. coli O157 (STEC/VTEC). Ask specifically about bloody stool so O157 selective media is used.
🔬Microscopy (OC&P)
Ova, cysts & parasites: Giardia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium. Send 3 separate samples as shedding is intermittent. Request in prolonged or travel-related diarrhoea.
☣️C. difficile toxin
SEPARATE test — must be requested by name. Two-step: GDH antigen + toxin (or toxin PCR then toxin EIA). Routine culture will NOT flag it.
2When to send a stool sample
Culture is indicated when a pathogen would change management or public-health action, not for every loose stool.
Bloody diarrhoea→Campylobacter, Shigella, E. coli O157 — test for STEC/Shiga toxin
Diarrhoea after antibiotics / hospital stay→Request C. difficile toxin
Recent travel→Parasites (OC&P) and consider enteric fever
Systemic illness, fever, or immunocompromise→Full culture + microscopy, low threshold to admit
Suspected outbreak / food handler→Culture and notify public health
Food poisoning and specific enteric pathogens are notifiable diseases — notify public health on clinical suspicion, don't wait for confirmation.
3Acting on the result
Most bacterial gastroenteritis is managed with rehydration alone; antibiotics are reserved for severe or high-risk disease.
C. diff positiveStop culprit antibioticOral vancomycin 1st-lineFidaxomicinIsolate
  • C. difficile: stop the offending antibiotic, oral vancomycin (first-line) or fidaxomicin, isolate the patient, and avoid antimotility agents. Severe disease can cause pseudomembranous colitis and toxic megacolon.
  • Campylobacter/Salmonella: usually self-limiting; antibiotics (e.g. clarithromycin/azithromycin for Campylobacter) only if severe or immunocompromised.
  • Giardia: metronidazole. Entamoeba histolytica: metronidazole plus a luminal agent.
📷 Image placeholder — endoscopic view of pseudomembranous colitis showing raised yellow-white adherent pseudomembranes on inflamed colonic mucosa, characteristic of C. difficile infection.
Infective diarrhoea ›
🚩
E. coli O157 (STEC/VTEC) produces Shiga toxin and can trigger haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) — the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, especially in children. In suspected or confirmed O157, DO NOT give antibiotics or antimotility agents — both may increase toxin release and the risk of HUS. Any child with bloody diarrhoea plus pallor, falling urine output, or bruising needs urgent bloods (FBC, film, U&E) and admission.
🎓 Exam pearl. C. difficile toxin and OC&P are separate tests that a routine bacterial culture will miss unless specifically requested. Testing = GDH antigen + toxin for C. diff, and 3 samples for parasites. The classic finals trap: a child with bloody diarrhoea and E. coli O157 — the answer is supportive care and monitoring for HUS, and never antibiotics or loperamide.
A throat swab is a microbiology test that detects group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes, GAS) — the main treatable bacterial cause of bacterial pharyngitis and tonsillitis. Crucially, most sore throats are viral and self-limiting, so in UK practice antibiotics are targeted using clinical scores rather than swabbing everyone.
1Score first, don't just swab
Because sore throats are usually viral, decide who needs antibiotics with CENTOR or FeverPAIN before reaching for a swab or a prescription.
Centor: Cough absentExudate on tonsilsNodes (tender anterior cervical)Temperature/fever
Low score (0–2)→Likely viral — safety-net, no antibiotics
High score (3–4)→Higher GAS probability — consider phenoxymethylpenicillin
FeverPAIN (Fever, Purulence, Attend rapidly ≤3 days, severe Inflammation, No cough/coryza) is the alternative NICE-endorsed score.
2What the swab actually tells you
A throat swab culture confirms GAS but has a 1–2 day delay; rapid antigen detection tests give a same-visit result. A key limitation: a positive swab does not distinguish active infection from carriage — asymptomatic GAS carriage is common, especially in children, so results must be read alongside the clinical picture.
  • Reserve swabs for uncertain, atypical, recurrent, or immunocompromised cases — not routine sore throats.
  • Give phenoxymethylpenicillin, not amoxicillin, if glandular fever (EBV) is possible.
3Think beyond strep — and warn the lab
Some diagnoses need special media or a heads-up to the lab, because they will not grow on routine culture.
🦠EBV (glandular fever)
Monospot/atypical lymphocytes; amoxicillin causes a maculopapular rash.
🦠Diphtheria
Grey pseudomembrane; unvaccinated/travellers — needs charcoal/tellurite medium; tell the lab.
🦠Gonococcal pharyngitis
Sexual history; needs specific media or NAAT, not routine swab.
4Why GAS matters: complications
Treating GAS is about preventing complications, not just symptom relief.
  • Scarlet fever — sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue; notifiable in the UK.
  • Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) — see Tonsillitis / quinsy ›
  • Post-streptococcal sequelae — rheumatic fever and post-strep glomerulonephritis.
🚩
Do not give amoxicillin/ampicillin when glandular fever (EBV) is possible — it triggers a florid maculopapular rash. Escalate urgently for quinsy (trismus, unilateral swelling, uvular deviation, "hot potato" voice) or any airway compromise (stridor, drooling, difficulty swallowing secretions). Remember scarlet fever and diphtheria are notifiable.
📷 Image placeholder — oropharynx with enlarged tonsils bearing white-yellow exudate and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, alongside a swab being taken from the tonsillar surface.
🎓 Exam pearl. Most sore throats are viral — use Centor/FeverPAIN to target antibiotics, not routine swabs. A positive swab cannot separate infection from carriage. Give phenoxymethylpenicillin (10 days), never amoxicillin if EBV is possible. Warn the lab for suspected diphtheria or gonococcal pharyngitis, and remember scarlet fever is notifiable.
A wound swab is a microbiology sample taken from an infected wound (surgical site infections, chronic ulcers, abscesses, or Cellulitis › with a skin breach) to identify the causative organism and its antibiotic sensitivities, guiding targeted therapy. The single most important concept for finals: treat the patient, not the swab — a positive result alone does not diagnose infection.
1Colonisation vs infection — the golden rule
Every open wound and chronic ulcer is colonised with bacteria. A positive swab therefore tells you what is present, not whether the wound is infected. Diagnose infection clinically, then use the swab to guide antibiotics.
Spreading erythemaWarmthIncreasing painPurulenceSystemic upset / fever
Clean, granulating ulcer, no signs of infection→Do NOT swab, do NOT treat
Spreading erythema + purulence + fever→Clinically infected → swab + start empirical Abx
Swabbing clinically uninfected wounds only grows colonisers and drives inappropriate antibiotic use.
2Sampling technique — quality matters
A superficial swab mostly grows surface colonisers and skin flora, giving misleading results. Improve yield:
  • Cleanse / debride the wound first to remove surface slough.
  • Swab the deep, advancing (leading) edge of the wound, using a rotating (Levine) technique over healthy-looking tissue.
  • Express and sample pus where present — send pus or tissue in preference to a dry surface swab.
  • Tissue biopsy or aspirated pus is superior to a surface swab.
Label with site, timing relative to antibiotics, and clinical details to help the lab interpret.
3Common organisms & interpretation
🦠Staph aureus (incl. MRSA)
Commonest wound & SSI pathogen. Check MRSA history/screen; sensitivities guide flucloxacillin vs MRSA-active agents.
⚡Beta-haemolytic strep (Group A / S. pyogenes)
Classic cause of cellulitis; can drive rapidly spreading and necrotising soft-tissue infection.
💧Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Moist wounds and burns; classic green discolouration and sweet odour.
🧫Anaerobes & mixed flora
Diabetic foot, pressure ulcers and bites — often polymicrobial; foul odour suggests anaerobes.
Interpret with sensitivities. In a clinically infected wound, start empirical antibiotics per local guidelines while awaiting results, then rationalise/escalate once cultures return.
🚩
Beware necrotising fasciitis: pain out of proportion to appearance, rapidly spreading erythema/dusky skin, systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, hypotension) and crepitus. This is a surgical emergency — do not wait for swab results; resuscitate, give broad-spectrum antibiotics and call surgery for urgent debridement.
📷 Image placeholder — describe an image: correct wound-swab technique showing a cleansed, debrided ulcer with the swab rotated over the deep advancing edge, alongside a clinically infected wound with spreading erythema and purulent discharge.
🎓 Exam pearl. If a stem gives you a positive wound swab but the wound looks clean with no clinical signs of infection, the answer is usually to NOT prescribe antibiotics — the swab reflects colonisation. Treat the patient, not the swab. And any wound with pain out of proportion + systemic toxicity is necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise — that trumps waiting for micro.
The Group B Streptococcus (GBS) swab is a recto-vaginal carriage screen for Streptococcus agalactiae, a common asymptomatic coloniser of the maternal vagina and rectum. GBS is the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis (sepsis, pneumonia and meningitis in the first week of life). Crucially, this is a colonisation test, not an infection test, and in the UK it feeds a risk-factor-based approach to intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) rather than universal screening.
1The swab & what it actually tests
A combined low vaginal + rectal (recto-vaginal) swab, ideally plated onto enriched (selective) culture media to maximise sensitivity for detecting carriage.
Low vaginal swabRectal swabEnriched selective media
GBS colonisation is transient and asymptomatic — a positive swab means carriage, not maternal or fetal infection. A woman can recolonise between an antenatal swab and delivery, which is why antenatal eradication is not the strategy.
2UK strategy: risk-factor-based, not universal
The UK (RCOG) does not offer universal antenatal GBS screening. Instead it identifies women who should be offered intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) to reduce vertical transmission during labour.
🧫GBS this pregnancy
Incidental positive vaginal/rectal swab, or GBS bacteriuria detected in the current pregnancy.
👶Previous GBS baby
A previous baby with GBS disease — a strong indication for IAP regardless of this pregnancy's swab.
⏱️Labour risk factors
Preterm labour, prolonged rupture of membranes, or intrapartum fever / suspected chorioamnionitis.
3IAP: the right drug at the right time
IAP is given during labour (intrapartum), not antenatally — treating carriage antenatally does not prevent recolonisation by the time of delivery.
No penicillin allergy→IV benzylpenicillin in labour
Penicillin-allergic→IV clindamycin
  • GBS bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated at the time and flags the need for IAP in labour.
  • IAP reduces early-onset GBS disease; it does not prevent late-onset disease.
4The newborn at risk
Babies at risk are observed and investigated. Early-onset GBS disease presents in the first week with:
  • Respiratory distress (grunting, tachypnoea, recession)
  • Temperature instability (fever or hypothermia)
  • Poor feeding, lethargy, or floppiness
It can progress rapidly to sepsis and meningitis. See Neonatal medicine › for the septic-neonate workup.
🚩
A septic-appearing neonate (respiratory distress, temperature instability, poor feeding or floppiness) in the first week — especially with maternal GBS or IAP risk factors — must be treated as early-onset GBS sepsis until proven otherwise: take cultures and start empirical IV antibiotics immediately. Do not wait for confirmation; early-onset GBS can progress to septic shock and meningitis within hours.
📷 Image placeholder — culture plate showing Group B Streptococcus colonies with a narrow zone of beta-haemolysis on blood/selective enrichment agar, alongside a labelled diagram of low-vaginal and rectal swab sampling sites.
🎓 Exam pearl. The UK is risk-factor-based, not universal screening — and the intervention is intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IV benzylpenicillin; clindamycin if penicillin-allergic), not antenatal eradication of carriage. Key IAP triggers: GBS this pregnancy (swab or bacteriuria), a previous GBS baby, preterm labour, prolonged rupture of membranes, or intrapartum fever. GBS is the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis — act on a septic neonate without delay.
MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & Microscopy:
The Gram stain is the rapid first-line microscopy step that classifies bacteria in minutes, giving an immediate clue to guide empirical antibiotics hours before culture and sensitivities return. The stain sequence is crystal violet → iodine (mordant) → decolourise (alcohol/acetone) → safranin counterstain. Gram-positive organisms retain the crystal violet and appear purple/blue (thick peptidoglycan wall); Gram-negative organisms lose it and take up safranin, appearing pink/red (thin wall).
1Read the colour first — positive vs negative
Colour reflects cell wall structure, not just a label. Gram-positive = purple because a thick peptidoglycan layer traps the crystal violet–iodine complex during decolourisation. Gram-negative = pink because the thin wall and outer membrane wash out and pick up the safranin counterstain.
Purple = Gram-positivePink = Gram-negative
2Then shape & arrangement → the classic organism
Work through a simple pipeline: colour → shape (cocci vs bacilli) → arrangement. This narrows you to a likely organism.
🔬GPC in clusters
Staphylococcus (catalase +) — e.g. S. aureus.
🔬GPC in chains/pairs
Streptococcus / Enterococcus (catalase −). Lancet diplococci = S. pneumoniae.
🔬GN diplococci
Neisseria — N. meningitidis (meningitis/sepsis); N. gonorrhoeae (intracellular diplococci in urethral pus).
🔬GN coccobacilli
Haemophilus influenzae — respiratory, epiglottitis.
🔬GP bacilli (rods)
Clostridium, Listeria, Bacillus, Corynebacterium.
🔬GN bacilli (rods)
Coliforms/Enterobacterales (E. coli, Klebsiella), Pseudomonas.
3CSF Gram stain in suspected meningitis
A CSF Gram stain gives a rapid organism clue while culture is pending:
GN diplococci→Meningococcus (N. meningitidis)
GP diplococci→Pneumococcus (S. pneumoniae)
GP bacilli→Listeria (elderly, neonates, immunosuppressed)
See also Meningitis / encephalitis ›
4Know the organisms Gram stain misses
Some clinically important bugs stain poorly or not at all — a negative Gram stain does not exclude infection:
  • Mycobacteria (TB) — waxy wall; use Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine (acid-fast).
  • Mycoplasma — no cell wall, so nothing to stain.
  • Treponema / spirochaetes — too thin; dark-field or serology.
  • Legionella, Chlamydia — intracellular/poorly staining; use culture, PCR or antigen.
🚩
In suspected meningitis or sepsis, give empirical antibiotics immediately — do not wait for the Gram stain, LP or CSF result. Blood cultures ideally before antibiotics, but antibiotics must never be delayed in a deteriorating or septic patient.
📷 Image placeholder — side-by-side high-power micrographs: purple Gram-positive cocci in clusters (Staphylococcus) versus pink Gram-negative bacilli (E. coli), with a third panel of pink intracellular diplococci within neutrophils (Neisseria).
🎓 Exam pearl. Purple = positive, pink = negative. Build the answer as colour → shape → arrangement: GPC clusters = Staph (catalase +), GPC chains = Strep (catalase −), GN diplococci in CSF = meningococcus, GP diplococci = pneumococcus. Remember the Gram-negatives that won't stain (TB, Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia, spirochaetes) — and that antibiotics come before the result in sepsis/meningitis.
The Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain detects acid-fast bacilli (AFB) — chiefly Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Mycobacteria have a waxy, mycolic-acid-rich cell wall that resists Gram staining, so a dedicated stain is needed. AFB appear as red/pink bacilli against a blue background and are called "acid-fast" because they resist decolourisation by acid-alcohol. Tuberculosis ›
1How the stain works
Three reagents are applied in sequence:
  • Carbol fuchsin (red) with heat — driven into the waxy wall, staining all cells red.
  • Acid-alcohol decolouriser — washes red out of everything EXCEPT acid-fast organisms, which hold onto the fuchsin.
  • Methylene blue counterstain — colours the background and non-acid-fast cells blue.
AFB = red/pink rodsBackground = blue
Auramine-phenol fluorescence microscopy is a more sensitive modern alternative used for screening — AFB fluoresce yellow-green under UV.
2Smear vs culture vs NAAT
AFB smear microscopy is rapid but insensitive — it needs a high bacillary load (roughly 5,000–10,000 organisms/mL). A negative smear does NOT exclude TB. Smear-positive pulmonary TB patients are the most infectious.
Smear +ve→Highly infectious — isolate
Smear −ve→Does NOT rule out TB — culture/NAAT
Send ≥3 sputum samples including an early-morning specimen; ZN can also be done on CSF, urine, pus and tissue.
  • Culture (Lowenstein-Jensen solid or liquid MGIT) is the gold standard and gives drug-susceptibility, but is slow (weeks).
  • NAAT / GeneXpert gives rapid confirmation and detects rifampicin resistance.
3Other acid-fast organisms
ZN is not entirely specific for mycobacteria — a few other organisms are acid-fast:
🦠M. tuberculosis
Classic AFB — red bacilli on sputum ZN.
🦠Nocardia
Partially acid-fast — modified ZN (weak decolouriser).
🦠Cryptosporidium / Cyclospora
Oocysts stain with modified ZN on stool.
🚩
A negative ZN smear does NOT rule out TB — always send culture and NAAT. A smear-positive pulmonary case is highly infectious: place the patient in a negative-pressure side room with airborne (respiratory) precautions, and remember TB is a notifiable disease — notify Public Health.
📷 Image placeholder — ZN-stained sputum smear at high power showing slender red/pink beaded bacilli (some in cords/clumps) scattered against a blue methylene-blue background of epithelial cells and debris.
🎓 Exam pearl. "Red rods on a blue background" = acid-fast bacilli, think TB. Remember: smear is fast but insensitive (needs ~5,000–10,000/mL), so a negative smear never excludes TB — culture (MGIT/LJ) is gold standard and gives sensitivities, while GeneXpert/NAAT gives rapid diagnosis plus rifampicin resistance. Smear-positive = most infectious → isolate and notify.
The India ink stain is a simple, rapid negative stain of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) used to visualise Cryptococcus neoformans — the classic cause of fungal meningitis in the immunocompromised, especially advanced HIV/AIDS (typically CD4 <100). The ink darkens the background, while the yeast's thick polysaccharide capsule excludes the ink, producing a clear halo around the budding organism. Crucially, it is insensitive — a negative result never excludes cryptococcal disease.
1What you actually see
India ink is a negative (background) stain: it does not enter the organism but stains the fluid around it. Against the dark background you see round, narrow-based budding yeasts surrounded by an unstained clear halo — the thick polysaccharide capsule refusing the ink. This capsule is the pathogen's key virulence factor and is the basis of both the stain appearance and antigen testing.
Encapsulated yeastClear haloNarrow-based budding
2Better tests — CrAg beats India ink
India ink is only ~50–80% sensitive even in HIV, so it must never be relied on alone. The preferred, more sensitive test is the cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) assay — the point-of-care lateral flow assay (LFA) or latex agglutination — performed on both CSF and serum, with excellent sensitivity and specificity. Fungal culture of CSF confirms the diagnosis and remains the gold standard.
🩸CrAg lateral flow
Most sensitive; rapid; CSF and serum; test of choice.
🔵India ink
Quick but insensitive — a negative result does not exclude.
🧫Fungal culture
Confirmatory gold standard; enables susceptibility testing.
3CSF findings & clinical picture
Cryptococcal meningitis is typically subacute: insidious headache, fever, mild meningism, confusion and cranial nerve palsies in an immunocompromised patient. Classic CSF pattern:
  • Raised opening pressure — a key prognostic and management issue
  • Lymphocytic pleocytosis (may be sparse in advanced HIV)
  • High protein, low/normal glucose
Encapsulated yeast + halo on ink→Confirm with CrAg + culture
Related: HIV › · Meningitis / encephalitis ›
4Treatment
Induction: IV amphotericin B + flucytosine, followed by fluconazole for consolidation and maintenance. Just as important, actively manage raised intracranial pressure with repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures (or drainage) — this reduces morbidity and mortality independently of antifungals. Optimise HIV care; watch for immune reconstitution syndrome if starting ART.
🚩
Suspect cryptococcal meningitis in any patient with HIV and CD4 <100 presenting with subacute headache and fever. A negative India ink is not reassuring — always send CrAg (lateral flow) and culture. A raised CSF opening pressure is a medical emergency requiring urgent therapeutic drainage / repeated LPs, as uncontrolled pressure is a leading cause of death and visual loss.
📷 Image placeholder — India ink preparation of CSF under light microscopy: a dark stippled background with round budding yeast cells, each surrounded by a bright clear unstained halo (the polysaccharide capsule).
🎓 Exam pearl. India ink shows an encapsulated yeast with a clear halo in CSF — pathognomonic buzzword for Cryptococcus. But remember it is insensitive: the higher-yield answer for diagnosis is CrAg lateral flow assay on CSF/serum, confirmed by culture. In management questions, the trap-avoiding answer is treating the raised opening pressure with therapeutic LPs alongside amphotericin B + flucytosine.
A KOH (potassium hydroxide) wet-mount is a rapid bedside/lab microscopy test for suspected superficial fungal infection. KOH digests keratin and human cellular debris (skin, nail, hair) but leaves the chitinous fungal wall intact — so fungal elements stand out against a cleared background. It is a fast, cheap first-line confirmation, but it shows fungal elements only, not the species.
1Sampling — go for the active edge
Collect from the site most likely to be teeming with fungus:
  • Skin — scrape the active scaly leading edge of the lesion with a blunt blade onto a slide.
  • Nail — clip the nail and collect subungual debris from the crumbling underside (highest yield in onychomycosis).
  • Hair — pluck affected hairs with the root (roots harbour the organism in tinea capitis).
Always send extra material for fungal culture at the same time — one collection, two tests.
2The prep & what KOH does
Place the sample on a slide, add a drop of 10–20% KOH, apply a coverslip and gently warm. Over a few minutes the KOH dissolves keratinocytes and debris (clearing the field) while the fungal wall resists — leaving fungal structures crisply visible under low then high power. An optional stain (e.g. chlorazol black or Parker ink) highlights the elements.
10–20% KOHWarm & waitLow → high power
3Reading the slide — pattern recognition
Match the microscopic picture to the likely organism:
🍄Dermatophyte (tinea)
Long, branching septate hyphae crossing keratinocyte outlines — corporis, pedis, cruris, capitis, unguium.
🍄Candida
Budding yeasts + pseudohyphae. On a vaginal wet mount supports vulvovaginal candidiasis.
🍝Malassezia
Short hyphae + round spores = “spaghetti and meatballs” in pityriasis versicolor.
Branching septate hyphae→Dermatophyte / tinea
Pseudohyphae + budding yeasts→Candida
“Spaghetti & meatballs”→Malassezia (versicolor)
4Adjuncts & limitations
Wood's lamp (UV) is a complementary bedside test: some tinea capitis fluoresces green, while coral-red fluorescence indicates erythrasma (Corynebacterium — bacterial, not fungal). Key limitation: KOH confirms the presence of fungus but not the species or sensitivity, and false negatives are common (operator-dependent, inadequate sample). A negative KOH does not exclude infection.
If suspicion persists despite a negative KOH, treat the culture — not the slide — as the arbiter.
See also Candidiasis ›
🚩
Never commit a patient to a long oral antifungal course — terbinafine or itraconazole for onychomycosis or tinea capitis — on KOH alone. KOH shows elements but not species, and these agents carry hepatotoxicity and drug-interaction risk. Confirm mycologically with culture before starting systemic treatment; a negative KOH with ongoing clinical suspicion warrants culture, not reassurance.
📷 Image placeholder — KOH wet-mount at high power showing long, branching, septate dermatophyte hyphae threading across a cleared field of faint keratinocyte outlines, alongside an inset of Candida budding yeasts with pseudohyphae.
🎓 Exam pearl. KOH = rapid confirmation of fungal elements; culture = the species (slower, needed for targeted/systemic therapy). Remember the three signatures — branching septate hyphae (dermatophyte), pseudohyphae + budding yeasts (Candida), “spaghetti & meatballs” (Malassezia/pityriasis versicolor). Always confirm nail/scalp disease before long oral antifungals.
CSF analysis after lumbar puncture is a classic finals pattern-recognition topic. LP is done at the L3/4–L4/5 interspace (below the spinal cord, which ends at ~L1/2). Always record the opening pressure, then send tubes for cell count & microscopy + Gram stain, protein, glucose (with a paired serum glucose — CSF glucose is normally ~⅔ / 60% of serum), culture, and PCR (meningococcal/pneumococcal in meningitis; HSV/enterovirus in encephalitis). Interpretation turns on three numbers — cells, protein, glucose — plus the clinical story.
1What to send & the normal CSF
Normal CSF is crystal clear ("gin clear"), with an opening pressure of 10–20 cmH₂O. Baseline reference values:
WCC <5 cells/µL0 neutrophilsProtein 0.15–0.45 g/LGlucose ≥60% serum
Always take a paired capillary/venous glucose at the same time — an isolated CSF glucose is uninterpretable. In suspected SAH also request spectrophotometry for xanthochromia; in suspected demyelination request oligoclonal bands (paired with serum).
2The three classic meningitis patterns
The exam-critical skill is separating bacterial, viral and TB/fungal meningitis on the CSF:
🦠Bacterial
Cloudy/turbid. Neutrophils (polymorphs) ↑↑. Protein high. Glucose low (<50% serum). Opening pressure ↑.
💧Viral
Clear. Lymphocytes ↑. Protein normal / mildly ↑. Glucose normal. Pressure usually normal.
🕸️TB / fungal
Fibrin web (TB). Lymphocytes ↑. Protein very high. Glucose low. Pressure ↑. Insidious onset.
Neutrophils + low glucose + high protein→bacterial until proven otherwise
Lymphocytes + normal glucose→viral (aseptic) meningitis / encephalitis
Lymphocytes + LOW glucose + very high protein→think TB or cryptococcal
Memory hook: low glucose = a "glucose-eating" organism → bacterial, TB or fungal. Normal glucose usually means viral.
3SAH — xanthochromia vs traumatic tap
If CT is negative but subarachnoid haemorrhage is still suspected (classic thunderclap headache), do an LP at ≥12 hours after headache onset — this allows time for red cells to lyse and haemoglobin to break down to bilirubin, producing xanthochromia (yellow CSF, confirmed on spectrophotometry).
Xanthochromia present→true SAH
Red cell count FALLS from tube 1 → 4, no xanthochromia→traumatic tap
4Two pattern must-knows: GBS & MS
  • Guillain-Barré syndrome — albuminocytological dissociation: raised protein with a normal cell count. Classically appears from ~week 1.
  • Multiple sclerosis — oligoclonal bands (IgG) present in CSF but not in paired serum, indicating intrathecal antibody production.
↑ protein, normal cells = GBSCSF-only oligoclonal bands = MS
🚩
In suspected bacterial meningitis or encephalitis, give empirical antibiotics ± IV aciclovir immediately — NEVER delay treatment for the LP or for imaging. Check for contraindications to LP first: signs of raised ICP, focal neurological deficit, seizures or reduced/fluctuating GCS mean CT the head before LP (risk of cerebral herniation / coning). Also avoid LP if coagulopathy, on anticoagulants, thrombocytopenia, or overlying skin infection.
📷 Image placeholder — describe an image: a comparison table/infographic of the three CSF meningitis patterns (bacterial vs viral vs TB) across appearance, predominant cell, protein and glucose, alongside a photo of turbid "cloudy" bacterial CSF and yellow xanthochromic CSF for SAH.
🎓 Exam pearl. The single most tested interpretation: neutrophils + low glucose + high protein = bacterial; lymphocytes + normal glucose = viral; lymphocytes + LOW glucose + very high protein = TB/fungal. Two dissociation traps: albuminocytological dissociation (↑protein, normal cells) = Guillain-Barré, and xanthochromia at ≥12h = SAH (distinguishes from a traumatic tap, where RBCs fall tube 1→4). Never let the LP delay antibiotics. See Meningitis / encephalitis › and Guillain-Barré syndrome ›.
MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular / PCR:
Syndromic multiplex PCR panels use nucleic acid amplification to detect the DNA/RNA of many pathogens from a single sample at once, with high sensitivity and specificity and a rapid turnaround (hours) — far faster than culture. They are grouped by clinical syndrome: respiratory, gastrointestinal (stool), and STI (plus CNS/meningitis panels). Their great strength — detecting nucleic acid — is also their key trap: a positive PCR is not proof of active, causative infection.
1The three common syndromic panels
Each panel targets the likely pathogens for a clinical presentation from one appropriate specimen.
🫁Respiratory (NP swab)
Influenza A/B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, parainfluenza, rhinovirus, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, plus atypicals (Mycoplasma, some Bordetella). Guides antivirals (oseltamivir) & isolation.
💩GI / stool
Bacteria (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, STEC/E. coli), viruses (norovirus, rotavirus) & parasites (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba).
🧬STI (& CNS)
Chlamydia, gonorrhoea, Trichomonas, Mycoplasma genitalium (from urine/swabs). A separate CNS/meningitis panel covers bacterial + viral causes on CSF.
2Why PCR beats culture — and where it wins
The advantages that make panels first-line in acute syndromic testing:
Rapid (hours)High sensitivity/specificityMultiple targets/sampleDetects fastidious/non-culturable
  • Detects fastidious or non-culturable organisms and those where prior antibiotics have killed viable bugs but left detectable nucleic acid.
  • Supports infection control: a rapid respiratory panel lets you isolate and cohort (e.g. influenza vs RSV vs COVID) and start antivirals quickly.
  • Aids antimicrobial stewardship — confirming a viral cause can stop unnecessary antibiotics.
3Interpreting the result — the exam trap
PCR detects nucleic acid, not viability. Always read it against the clinical picture.
Persistent positive after recovery→Prolonged shedding (norovirus, SARS-CoV-2) — not ongoing active infection
Positive but asymptomatic target→Colonisation/carriage, or a bystander — not necessarily the cause
Need to guide antibiotic choice→Panels give NO susceptibilities — send culture for sensitivities
A positive PCR is not automatically the diagnosis — correlate with symptoms, timing and other results. Many respiratory viruses covered here are reviewed in more depth under viral infections.
Viral infections ›
🚩
A positive panel is not a licence to over- or under-treat. Panels provide no antibiotic sensitivities, so always send culture when susceptibility matters (e.g. bacteraemia, resistant organisms). Use rapid respiratory results for isolation/cohorting and antivirals, and use viral confirmation for stewardship — but never let PCR detection of shedding or carriage drive unnecessary antimicrobials.
📷 Image placeholder — a labelled schematic of a multiplex PCR workflow: one nasopharyngeal/stool specimen → nucleic acid extraction → multiple target-specific primer/probe reactions amplifying in parallel → a results grid showing several pathogens reported positive/negative within hours.
🎓 Exam pearl. Multiplex PCR is fast, sensitive and multi-target, but detects nucleic acid, not viable organisms — so it cannot distinguish active infection from shedding or carriage and gives no antibiotic sensitivities. If a stem asks what culture still adds over a panel, the answer is susceptibility testing (and viable-organism/quantitative confirmation). Rapid respiratory panels are prized for infection control and antiviral decisions.
A NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) is the gold-standard, first-line test for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It amplifies organism DNA/RNA, giving very high sensitivity and specificity — but the key exam trap is that a NAAT gives no antibiotic sensitivities, so a gonorrhoea culture must still be taken before treatment. Chlamydia › Gonorrhoea ›
1Which sample from which site
Sample site is dictated by sex and exposure, not convenience.
Women: self-taken vulvovaginal swabMen: first-catch (first-void) urine
In men use the first-catch urine, NOT a midstream sample — the first fraction carries the highest organism load.
MSM / receptive anal or oral exposure→add rectal & pharyngeal swabs
Genital-only testing misses extragenital infection — always sample per exposure history.
2Chlamydia — often silent, so screen
Chlamydia is frequently asymptomatic, especially in women, so diagnosis relies on screening rather than symptoms.
  • National Chlamydia Screening Programme — opportunistic testing in sexually active under-25s.
  • First-line treatment is doxycycline (azithromycin as an alternative, e.g. in pregnancy).
  • Always arrange partner notification / contact tracing.
3Gonorrhoea — NAAT confirms, culture guides treatment
NAAT confirms the diagnosis, but a positive NAAT gives no sensitivities. Because of rising antimicrobial resistance, take a culture (charcoal swab) from the infected site BEFORE starting antibiotics.
🧬NAAT
Detects DNA/RNA — highly sensitive, confirms diagnosis, but NO antibiotic sensitivities.
🧫Culture (charcoal swab)
Taken BEFORE treatment for antimicrobial sensitivity testing — essential with rising resistance.
Treat gonorrhoea with IM ceftriaxone (guided by sensitivities); a test of cure is recommended.
🚩
Untreated infection is not benign: chlamydia and gonorrhoea cause pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility, plus disseminated gonococcal infection and ophthalmia neonatorum in vertical transmission. Always confirm partner notification is done — treating the index patient alone leaves reinfection and onward spread untouched.
📷 Image placeholder — sampling algorithm: a self-taken vulvovaginal swab (women) and a first-catch urine pot (men) feeding into a NAAT, with a separate charcoal culture swab shown branching off for gonorrhoea before antibiotics.
🎓 Exam pearl. NAAT is first-line for both chlamydia and gonorrhoea. In women the sample of choice is a self-taken vulvovaginal swab; in men it is a first-catch urine (not midstream). For gonorrhoea, a positive NAAT gives no sensitivities, so always take a culture (charcoal swab) before treatment — and sample rectal/pharyngeal sites per exposure.
A viral swab for PCR is the investigation of choice to confirm and distinguish herpes simplex (HSV-1/2) from varicella-zoster (VZV) in a vesicular rash. The swab is taken from the base of a deroofed vesicle, and PCR is rapid, highly sensitive and specific, and types the virus — so it has largely replaced older methods (viral culture, Tzanck smear, direct immunofluorescence).
1What it is & how to sample
Choose a fresh, fluid-filled vesicle, deroof it, and firmly swab the base and fluid — not a dry crust or a healing lesion (low viral yield). Send in viral transport medium.
Result within hours to ~1 dayTypes HSV-1 vs HSV-2 vs VZV
PCR can also be run on other samples depending on the clinical question:
  • CSF — suspected HSV encephalitis
  • Ocular / corneal swab — HSV keratitis
  • Neonatal surface & systemic samples — neonatal HSV
A crusted or dry lesion gives a false-negative — always deroof a fresh vesicle.
2When to use it (clinical scenarios)
Genital / orolabial vesicles→Confirm HSV & type (HSV-1 vs HSV-2)
Chickenpox vs shingles→VZV PCR; dermatomal = zoster
Atypical rash / immunocompromised→PCR distinguishes HSV vs VZV vs other
Unwell child, eczema + monomorphic erosions→HSV PCR confirms eczema herpeticum
3Key high-yield presentations
🦠Eczema herpeticum
Widespread HSV on eczematous skin — monomorphic punched-out erosions, unwell/febrile child. Dermatological emergency.
🧠HSV encephalitis
Fever, confusion, seizures, temporal lobe change — CSF HSV PCR, but start aciclovir first.
👁️Ophthalmic zoster / keratitis
Zoster on nose tip (Hutchinson's sign) or HSV dendritic ulcer — urgent ophthalmology.
⚠️Disseminated zoster
Multi-dermatomal / visceral VZV in the immunocompromised — admit for IV aciclovir.
See also: Viral infections ›
🚩
For sight- or life-threatening presentations — eczema herpeticum, HSV encephalitis, or ophthalmic involvement — start empirical aciclovir immediately and do NOT wait for the PCR result. The swab confirms the diagnosis but must never delay treatment. Also watch for bacterial superinfection in eczema herpeticum.
📷 Image placeholder — describe an image: a clinician deroofing a fresh vesicle with a needle and firmly swabbing its base, with a viral transport medium tube alongside; inset shows monomorphic punched-out erosions of eczema herpeticum on eczematous skin.
🎓 Exam pearl. Vesicle-base swab for viral PCR is the test of choice and distinguishes HSV from VZV, having replaced the Tzanck smear and culture. Always sample a fresh, deroofed vesicle (crusts give false negatives). In eczema herpeticum, HSV encephalitis, or ophthalmic disease, treat empirically with aciclovir — do not wait for the result.
Meningococcal and pneumococcal PCR detect the DNA of Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae in EDTA blood and/or CSF in suspected meningitis and meningococcal sepsis. Their great advantage is that they stay positive even after antibiotics have been given — precisely when blood and CSF cultures have often become sterile.
1What it is & what it detects
A nucleic acid amplification test (PCR) that amplifies bacterial DNA rather than growing live organisms. Send an EDTA (purple-top) blood sample for meningococcal/pneumococcal PCR in every suspected case, and add CSF PCR if an LP is safely obtainable. PCR can also serogroup meningococcus (e.g. B, W, Y), which directly informs the vaccination and public-health response.
EDTA blood PCRCSF PCRSerogrouping
2Why it matters — positive after antibiotics
In suspected meningococcal disease you must give antibiotics immediately and never delay for LP or investigations. Pre-hospital IM benzylpenicillin and early hospital ceftriaxone rapidly sterilise blood and CSF cultures, so cultures are frequently negative ("culture-negative meningococcal disease"). Because PCR detects DNA, not live bacteria, it remains positive for days afterwards and becomes the main way to confirm the organism retrospectively and to trigger public-health action.
Antibiotics given before LP→Cultures sterile, but PCR still positive
3Interpreting the result
  • Positive — confirms the pathogen; serogroup informs contacts & vaccine strategy.
  • Negative — does not exclude disease if sampled very early or with low bacterial load; treat on clinical grounds.
  • Gives no antibiotic sensitivities — culture is still needed for susceptibility testing where obtainable.
Complements CSF microscopy/culture and blood cultures — it does not replace them.
🧠Meningococcal PCR
Confirms N. meningitidis; serogroups for public health & contact prophylaxis.
🫁Pneumococcal PCR
Confirms S. pneumoniae when cultures are sterile after antibiotics.
🚩
Give parenteral antibiotics at first suspicion — do NOT delay for LP or investigations. Non-blanching rash + unwell child in the community → IM benzylpenicillin now, then blue-light transfer. Always take an EDTA blood sample for meningococcal/pneumococcal PCR. Meningococcal disease is a notifiable disease: notify public health and arrange contact prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin) for close contacts.
📷 Image placeholder — EDTA purple-top blood tube beside a CSF sample pot, with an arrow to a PCR thermal cycler; caption "DNA detected despite sterile cultures."
🎓 Exam pearl. If a stem gives a septic child with a non-blanching rash who received benzylpenicillin before arrival and now has negative blood and CSF cultures, the single best test to confirm the organism is EDTA blood (and CSF) meningococcal PCR — it stays positive post-antibiotics. Remember it is notifiable and drives contact prophylaxis. See Meningitis / encephalitis › and Sepsis ›.
MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypicals & Sensitivit:
Confirming active tuberculosis is microbiological: run a battery of tests on a good respiratory sample — ideally ≥1 (better 3) early-morning sputum samples; use induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage if none can be produced, and early-morning urine, tissue or CSF for extrapulmonary disease. The three active-disease tests answer three different questions: AFB smear = is the patient infectious now? Culture = the gold-standard confirmation and drug susceptibilities; GeneXpert/NAAT = a rapid answer that also flags rifampicin (MDR-TB) resistance. Never confuse these with latent-TB tests (Mantoux/IGRA), which prove immune sensitisation only.
1AFB smear — fast, tells you infectivity, but insensitive
A Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine (fluorescent) stain looks for acid-fast bacilli. It is the quickest test (same day) and identifies the most infectious patients — a smear-positive case has the highest bacillary load and greatest transmission risk. Its weaknesses are critical: it needs a high bacillary load (~10,000 organisms/mL) so sensitivity is low, and it is not specific for M. tuberculosis — non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) also stain acid-fast.
Same daySmear-positive = most infectiousLow sensitivityNot species-specific
A NEGATIVE smear does NOT exclude TB — treat clinically and wait for culture/NAAT.
2Culture — the gold standard (sensitive + drug susceptibilities), but slow
Culture on Löwenstein-Jensen solid medium or liquid MGIT is the gold standard: it is the most sensitive test, confirms the species, and — crucially — provides drug-susceptibility testing (DST) to guide the regimen. The catch is that M. tuberculosis is very slow-growing:
  • Liquid (MGIT): ~1–3 weeks
  • Solid (LJ): up to 6–8 weeks
Need to confirm species + guide drug choice→Culture is definitive, but do not wait on it to start treatment
3GeneXpert / NAAT — rapid DNA + rifampicin-resistance flag
The GeneXpert MTB/RIF nucleic-acid amplification test detects M. tuberculosis DNA within hours and simultaneously detects mutations in the rpoB gene that confer rifampicin resistance — a surrogate marker for multi-drug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). It is recommended for rapid diagnosis, to guide early treatment and infection control, and especially where drug resistance or HIV is a concern.
🧫AFB smear
Hours, shows infectivity, low sensitivity, not specific
🥇Culture (LJ / MGIT)
Gold standard: species + drug susceptibilities, but 1–8 weeks
🧬GeneXpert / NAAT
Hours: MTB DNA + rifampicin (MDR-TB) resistance via rpoB
4Do NOT confuse with latent-TB tests
The tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA, e.g. QuantiFERON) detect immune sensitisation to TB antigens. They are tests for latent TB infection — they do NOT diagnose active disease and cannot distinguish latent from active TB. Only smear, culture and NAAT confirm active disease.
Active disease suspected→Smear + culture + NAAT (not Mantoux/IGRA)
Screening a contact / immune sensitisation→Mantoux or IGRA
🚩
TB is a notifiable disease — notify public health and arrange contact tracing. Place any suspected pulmonary case in airborne / respiratory isolation (negative-pressure side room), as a smear-positive patient is the most infectious. Start empirical RIPE (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) on clinical suspicion — a negative smear does not exclude TB — and involve TB services.
📷 Image placeholder — Ziehl-Neelsen stained sputum smear showing beaded red acid-fast bacilli against a blue counterstained background, alongside a Löwenstein-Jensen slope with buff, rough, dry M. tuberculosis colonies.
🎓 Exam pearl. Match the test to the question: smear = fast + infectivity (but low sensitivity, non-specific — negative does NOT exclude TB); culture = gold standard, gives species + drug susceptibilities but slow (weeks); NAAT/GeneXpert = rapid MTB detection AND rifampicin-resistance (MDR-TB) flag. Mantoux/IGRA test latent infection, not active disease. Remember: notifiable, airborne isolation, smear-positive = most infectious. See Tuberculosis ›
Urinary antigen tests are rapid immunoassays (results in ~15–60 min) that detect microbial antigen excreted in the urine. In pneumonia they are used to identify two specific pathogens fast: Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Their standout advantage over culture is that they stay positive even after antibiotics have been started — but each detects only a narrow target, so a negative result never excludes the infection. Used to guide targeted therapy in moderate–severe Pneumonia ›.
🧫Legionella antigen
Detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1 ONLY — the commonest cause of Legionnaires'. Negative ≠ excluded.
🧪Pneumococcal antigen
Detects S. pneumoniae C-polysaccharide. Useful when cultures negative or already treated.
1Legionella urinary antigen
Detects Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 only — so a negative test does NOT exclude Legionella of other serogroups or species. Stays positive for days to weeks, even after antibiotics. Indicated in:
  • Severe or non-responding community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)
  • Suggestive features — hyponatraemia, deranged LFTs, confusion, diarrhoea
  • Travel / hotel / spa exposure, or outbreak investigation
CAP + hyponatraemia + diarrhoea + recent travel→Send Legionella urinary antigen
Legionella is NOT covered by beta-lactams alone — treat with a macrolide (clarithromycin) or fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin).
2Pneumococcal urinary antigen
Detects the S. pneumoniae C-polysaccharide antigen. Rapid and remains positive after antibiotics, so it is valuable when blood/sputum cultures are negative or the patient has already been treated. Limitations:
  • Can be falsely positive with recent pneumococcal colonisation or recent vaccination
  • Less reliable in children (high nasopharyngeal carriage causes false positives)
3Why they matter — and their limits
Recommended in moderate–severe CAP (CURB-65 driven). Key value:
Stay positive post-antibioticsEnable targeted / narrowed therapyAntimicrobial stewardship
Limitations to state in an exam:
  • Give NO antibiotic sensitivities (unlike culture)
  • Detect only these specific organisms/serotypes — a negative result does not exclude infection
🚩
Legionnaires' disease is NOTIFIABLE. It needs a macrolide or quinolone — it is not covered by a beta-lactam alone, so empirical amoxicillin will fail. Actively test in severe or non-responding CAP, especially with hyponatraemia, deranged LFTs, confusion or diarrhoea. Remember both antigens stay positive after antibiotics, but the Legionella test detects only serogroup 1 — a negative does not exclude Legionnaires'.
📷 Image placeholder — a lateral-flow urinary antigen test cassette showing a control line plus a positive test line, labelled to contrast a rapid bedside immunoassay with a slower agar culture plate.
🎓 Exam pearl. Both urinary antigen tests remain positive after antibiotics are started (their key edge over culture) but give no sensitivities. Legionella antigen detects serogroup 1 only — negative does not exclude Legionella. Classic Legionnaires' vignette: severe CAP with hyponatraemia, deranged LFTs, diarrhoea/confusion and recent travel/hotel → it is notifiable and needs a macrolide/quinolone, not a beta-lactam alone.
Cold agglutinins are IgM autoantibodies that clump red cells at low temperatures. They are the classic (now largely historical, non-specific) clue to Mycoplasma pneumoniae atypical pneumonia and can trigger a cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (cold AIHA). Present in a substantial minority of cases, they are a supportive hint only — never the confirmatory test. See Pneumonia ›
1What cold agglutinins are & why Mycoplasma
Cold agglutinins are IgM antibodies (usually anti-I) that bind and agglutinate red cells in cooler peripheral blood, then fix complement, causing an intravascular/extravascular cold AIHA. In Mycoplasma pneumoniae, molecular mimicry between the organism and the red-cell I antigen drives their production. The picture: a young, previously well patient with an atypical pneumonia who develops anaemia and jaundice.
Blood cools in the periphery→IgM agglutinates RBCs + fixes complement → haemolysis
IgM cold antibodyAnti-I specificityComplement-mediated
2Recognising the Mycoplasma pneumonia
An atypical pneumonia: young, previously well patients, gradual onset, dry cough, prominent extrapulmonary features, and a chest X-ray that often looks worse than the clinical exam. It circulates in epidemics roughly every few years. Crucially, Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so beta-lactams (penicillins/cephalosporins) do NOT work.
🧫Macrolide
First line — e.g. clarithromycin (or azithromycin/erythromycin).
💊Tetracycline
Alternative — doxycycline. Both bypass the missing cell wall.
🚫Beta-lactams fail
No cell wall ⇒ penicillins & cephalosporins are ineffective.
3Confirming the diagnosis — NOT cold agglutinins
Cold agglutinins are a non-specific, supportive clue only. They can also be positive with EBV, other infections, and lymphoproliferative disease, so they cannot confirm Mycoplasma. Confirm with:
  • Mycoplasma serology — paired acute and convalescent antibody titres showing a rise.
  • PCR of a respiratory sample (throat swab/sputum) — rapid and specific.
Practical lab note: cold agglutinins can interfere with the FBC (spurious red-cell indices, visible clumping). The sample may need warming to 37°C before analysis.
🚩
Watch for the extrapulmonary complications of Mycoplasma: cold AIHA (anaemia + jaundice + haemolysis), mucocutaneous disease (erythema multiforme / Stevens–Johnson-like), neurological involvement (encephalitis, Guillain–Barré), myringitis bullosa, and arthralgia. Severe haemolysis or neurological signs warrant urgent escalation.
📷 Image placeholder — describe an image: a peripheral blood film showing red-cell agglutination (clumps of RBCs at room temperature) alongside a chest X-ray of atypical pneumonia with patchy consolidation looking worse than the clinical picture.
🎓 Exam pearl. Young patient + dry cough + CXR worse than exam + anaemia/jaundice = think Mycoplasma with cold AIHA. Remember: cold agglutinins are a hint, not proof (confirm with serology or PCR), and because Mycoplasma has no cell wall, treat with a macrolide or doxycycline — beta-lactams fail.
Helicobacter pylori is a gram-negative, urease-producing bacterium that colonises the gastric mucosa, causing chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, and is a risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma. In uninvestigated dyspepsia (after alarm-feature triage), NICE recommends a non-invasive test-and-treat strategy. The single most examined pitfall is the false negative: PPIs and recent antibiotics suppress the organism and must be stopped before testing. See Peptic ulcer disease ›
1The three tests: how each works
All three exploit the fact that H. pylori produces urease, which splits urea into ammonia and CO2.
🌬️Urea Breath Test (UBT)
Patient swallows 13C-labelled urea; bacterial urease releases labelled CO2 detected in exhaled breath. Non-invasive, high sensitivity/specificity. Preferred test of cure.
🧫Stool Antigen Test
Detects H. pylori antigen in faeces. Non-invasive, good sensitivity/specificity. Usable for diagnosis and test of cure.
🔬CLO / Rapid Urease Test
Invasive — antral biopsy at endoscopy placed on urea/indicator gel; urease raises pH → colour change. Used when scoping anyway. Histology/culture are alternatives.
CLO = Campylobacter-Like Organism test (older name for H. pylori).
2The false-negative trap (STOP the drugs)
PPIs, recent antibiotics and bismuth suppress H. pylori, causing false-negative UBT, stool antigen AND CLO results.
Stop PPI ≥ 2 weeksStop antibiotics/bismuth ≥ 4 weeks
Serology (antibody)→stays positive after eradication — cannot distinguish current from past infection; NOT recommended for diagnosis or test of cure
3Test of cure after eradication
Confirm eradication with a urea breath test (or stool antigen), at least 4–8 weeks after completing therapy.
  • Standard triple therapy: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin (or metronidazole) for 7 days.
  • Recheck test of cure especially in ulcer disease, MALT lymphoma or persistent symptoms.
  • Never use serology for test of cure — it remains positive.
🚩
Do not simply test-and-treat if alarm features are present. Dysphagia, unexplained weight loss, GI bleeding (haematemesis/melaena), persistent vomiting, iron-deficiency anaemia, an epigastric mass, or age ≥ 55 with new-onset persistent dyspepsia warrant an urgent 2-week-wait upper GI endoscopy to exclude malignancy.

🎓 Exam pearl. Non-invasive tests (UBT / stool antigen) are first-line for diagnosis and for test of cure. Any positive urease-based or antigen test can be falsely negative if the patient is on a PPI (stop ≥ 2 weeks) or recent antibiotics/bismuth (stop ≥ 4 weeks). Serology is never used for test of cure because it stays positive after eradication. Reserve CLO/biopsy for patients already undergoing endoscopy, and refer alarm features on the 2-week-wait pathway rather than test-and-treat.
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) is the step that turns a positive culture into a targeted prescription. It answers the clinical question: which antibiotic will actually treat this organism? Crucially, AST needs a viable isolate from culture — molecular tests (PCR) and antigen tests confirm the organism but give NO sensitivities. The quantitative anchor is the MIC, compared against EUCAST breakpoints to report S / I / R.
1MIC & breakpoints — the numbers that drive prescribing
The Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) is the lowest concentration of an antibiotic that inhibits visible growth of the organism — the quantitative measure of susceptibility (a lower MIC = more susceptible). Contrast the MBC (minimum bactericidal concentration) = lowest concentration that kills 99.9% of the inoculum. The lab compares the MIC against published breakpoints — in the UK these are set by EUCAST — to sort the organism into a reporting category.
MIC = inhibits growthMBC = kills 99.9%EUCAST breakpoints (UK)
🟢S — Susceptible
High likelihood of therapeutic success at standard dosing.
🟠I — Susceptible, Increased exposure
Success likely with a higher dose or where the drug concentrates at the site.
🔴R — Resistant
High likelihood of failure even at maximum dose — do not use.
EUCAST redefined "I" as Susceptible, Increased exposure — it is no longer "Intermediate". Labs report a selective panel of agents, not every drug, to steer prescribing and stewardship.
2Methods — how the lab measures susceptibility
Several techniques generate S/I/R, from cheap plates to gene detection:
🧫Disc diffusion (Kirby-Bauer)
Antibiotic-impregnated discs on an agar lawn; a larger zone of inhibition diameter = more susceptible.
📏Gradient strip (E-test)
Plastic strip with an antibiotic gradient gives a direct MIC where the elliptical zone intersects the strip.
🤖Automated broth microdilution
Machines (e.g. VITEK) grow the isolate across drug dilutions and read MICs rapidly.
🧬Molecular resistance genes
Detect resistance directly — mecA (MRSA), rpoB (rifampicin-resistant TB), carbapenemase genes.
Bigger zone / lower MIC→more susceptible → likely reported S
PCR / antigen positive, no isolate→organism identified but no sensitivities
3Interpretation — "S" on the plate ≠ cure in the patient
A result of Susceptible in vitro does not guarantee clinical cure. Always factor in the site of infection and antibiotic penetration:
  • Penetration: the CNS, bone, prostate and biofilms are hard to reach — an agent that is "S" may still under-dose the target site.
  • Source control: an abscess needs drainage, an infected line needs removal — no antibiotic sterilises undrained pus.
  • Right drug-bug-site combo: e.g. daptomycin is inactivated by surfactant so is useless in pneumonia despite in-vitro activity.
  • De-escalate: switch from empirical broad-spectrum cover to targeted narrow-spectrum therapy once sensitivities return — the core of antimicrobial stewardship.
Resistance concepts that make AST and stewardship matter: MRSA (mecA), ESBL and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales, VRE, and MDR-TB.
🚩
De-escalate to narrow spectrum once sensitivities return, and escalate to microbiology / ID for resistant organisms — MRSA, ESBL, carbapenemase-producers, VRE, MDR-TB. Never keep a patient on broad-spectrum empirical cover when a targeted agent is available, and remember an abscess or infected device needs source control regardless of the sensitivity report.
